prompt: Many patients do not follow the advice they are given by their doctors. Why does this happen? What are the consequences of this behaviour?
essay:
Patients who ignore medical advice are usually described as non-compliant, a word that locates the failure entirely in them. It is more useful to ask what the advice looked like from the receiving end, because most of the behaviour becomes intelligible as soon as you do.

Three things account for the bulk of it. The first is that the reasoning is rarely transmitted. A consultation compressed into a few minutes can deliver an instruction but not a rationale, and an instruction without a rationale has no defence against the moment the symptoms stop. Nobody abandons a course of antibiotics in defiance of the evidence; they abandon it because feeling better is concrete and the surviving bacteria are not.

The second inverts the ordinary structure of a decision: the costs of a statin or a course of chemotherapy arrive today and are felt in the body, while the benefit is a statistical event that may never happen and, if the drug works, is indistinguishable from nothing happening at all. The third applies wherever the prescription is behavioural — lose weight, stop drinking — and asks a person to sustain, alone and indefinitely, a change that their surroundings are organised against.

The consequences run outwards from there. Individually, a half-treated illness tends to return in a form that is harder to manage, so a decision that avoided a fortnight of nausea buys a week in hospital. Collectively, unfinished antibiotic courses are among the most reliable ways of breeding resistant bacteria, which shifts the cost onto people who made no decision at all. And the cheapest resource in medicine — a patient who believes what they are told — is depleted a little each time, because a doctor who expects to be ignored explains less, and advice explained badly is ignored more.

The loop closes, in other words, on the cause, which suggests that the treatable part of this problem is not the patient's discipline but the five minutes in which the reason was never given.
title: Why patients ignore their doctors
